nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Common Name:  Yellowfin menhaden
Scientific Name: Brevoortia smithi

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Phylum:	Chordata
	Class:		Osteichthyes
	Order:		Clupeiformes
	Family:	Clupeidae

Other Common Names:  Yellowfin shad (307); yellowtail (831), Atlantic finescale (264), shad (664), bug fish (835).

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial:  This species apparently does not contribute appreciably to the commercial menhaden catch (823).  Reintjes (1052) reported annual catches of around 10,000 lbs. along the southwest Florida coast, and combined landings for both coasts of about 500,000 lbs. during the early 1960's.  State of Florida landings data (902) reported statewide menhaden landings as 21,767,964 lbs in 1987, but lump all four species found in Florida as menhaden. It is likely B. smithi makes up only a small fraction of statewide landings.  The catch is sold fresh or as crab bait on the both the east and west coasts of Florida (1052 1055).  Marketed mostly fresh, the flesh is claimed to be more palatable and less oily than B. tyrannus (791).

Recreational:  Occasionally caught in cast nets and used as crab bait.

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall:  The yellowfin menhaden is found from Chandeleur Sound, Louisiana eastward and southward to the Caloosahatchee River, Florida with distribution continuous around Florida to as far north as North Carolina (788 791 822 823 300).  Levi (828) reported the collection of this species off Grand Bahama Island.

Within Study Area:  This species has been reported from Chandeleur Sound, Louisiana to Key West Florida (823 1052).  Relatively abundant on the Florida west coast from Florida Bay to the panhandle (823), and most abundant from Cape Sable to Sarasota (829).  On the Atlantic coast, from North Carolina to Jupiter Inlet, Florida (829 887 997 1009).  Apparently rare between West Palm Beach and Miami (823), with a possible break between Biscayne Bay and Florida Bay (791 829).  On the Florida east coast, most abundant from Cape Kennedy to the St. Lucie Inlet (823).  Dahlberg (823) stated that B. smithi was making a genetic introgression into the Indian River Lagoon.

Mobility and Migration:
Life Mode:  Generally an inshore or bay form with migration limited or absent (823).  Some collection data suggest a possible northern distribution in late summer, with a southward movement of the species during the spawning season (737 831).  Known to migrate up large rivers (835).

Eggs and larvae: are planktonic (824).
Juvenile and adult: are pelagic (823) and aggregate in loose scattered schools (829).
Adult: school where common, and large numbers have been collected in single net hauls around Florida (823).

nodes.title: BENTHIC HABITAT
nodes.body:
Habitat Type:  The yellowfin menhaden is a neritic species (823 1055).  Larvae and juveniles probably occur in all inland tidal waters of the study area (264 831).  Adults frequent estuaries and tidal embayments and also enter fresh waters during a portion of the year (791).  All are caught within the ten fathom curve (737 829).

Substrate:  Presumably occur over sand and mud bottoms in nearshore and estuarine waters.  Juveniles and adults collected over shell bottoms and algae in the Ten Thousand Islands area of southwest Florida (1054).

nodes.title: Physical/Chemical
nodes.body:
Temperature:  Eggs have been collected in waters with surface temperatures ranging from as low as 16.4 C (830) to 25.4 C (827).  Juveniles were collected in Tampa Bay at temperatures ranging from 18.0 C to 30.3 C (664).  Wang and Raney (789) collected a single juvenile in the Caloosahatchee River, Florida at a temperature of 17.0 C.  B. smithi were not killed in freezes in Florida (236).

Salinity:  Eggs recorded at salinities as low as 20.1 ppt (830) but also up to 33.0 ppt (827).  Juveniles have been found in salinities of 1.89 ppt in the Caloosahatchee River, Florida (264), and Springer and Woodburn (664) collected juveniles in salinities ranging from 3.7 ppt to 25.5 ppt in Tampa Bay.  Wang and Raney (789) took a single juvenile in Lemon Bay, Florida at a salinity of 27.2 ppt.  Both juveniles and adults were taken in salinities ranging from 3.0 ppt to 36.0 ppt in the Ten Thousand Islands area of southwest Florida; the largest number were taken at salinities ranging from 27.0 ppt to 30.0 ppt (1054).  Adults have been taken in Sarasota Bay at salinities as high as 31.6 ppt (664).  Adults are also known to enter fresh waters (791 835) and were classified as euryhaline by Gunter (261).

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body:
Reproductive Mode:  Oviparous.  Reproduction is sexual with separate sexes and external fertilization.

Mating/Spawning: Spawning occurs nearshore, apparently in inland tidal waters (823 829).  This species is a winter spawner (December and March);  A February through March spawning period has been  suggested for the Indian River, Florida area (791), and Springer and Woodburn (664) also thought that spawning occurs in the spring in Tampa Bay.  The presence of ripe females in February and March off southern Florida also suggests an early spring spawning period (737).  Spawning occurs later than in the Gulf menhaden (October and March) (664 802 824 831).  A sex ratio of nearly 1:1 was reported for fish collected off southern Florida (737).

Fecundity:  No information available.

nodes.title: Length Range
nodes.body:
Eggs and larvae:  Egg diameters range between 1.21 - 1.48 mm (827).  The time for hatching varies with temperature;  at 19.5 C to 21.5 C hatching occurs in 38 to 39 hours (824), above 22.0 C hatching occurs in less than 24 hours (827).  Eggs from the east Florida coast hatched in 46 hours at 18.0 C, 34 hours at 21.0 C, and 26 hours at 26.0 C (824 830).
Larvae: at hatching is about 3.0 mm SL (827).  Larvae begin transforming at around 14.0 mm SL with transformation complete between 20 and 23 mm SL (827).  Growth appears to be very rapid (831).  At 26 C in the laboratory, larvae grew 0.45 mm/day until day 20 (827)
Juveniles and adults:  Juveniles reach 160 mm FL by the end of their first summer and approximately 220 mm by the end of their second summer.  Sexual maturity is apparently attained during the second winter for most individuals (831). Mature adults differ from young adults in that their scales are more strongly serrated and their bodies are not as deep.  The largest recorded specimen is 330 mm TL (307).

nodes.title: FOOD HABITS
nodes.body: The yellowfin menhaden is a filter feeder.  The diet for this species consists of phytoplankton, detritus and small zooplankton strained from the water column (1055).  Hildebrand (307) reported the presence of diatoms and sponge spicules in B. smithi stomachs.

nodes.title: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
nodes.body:
Predation: B. smithi is host to the parasitic copepod, Lernaeenicus radians (307).  Called bug fish because, when in rivers, almost all individuals have parasitic crustaceans in the roof of the mouth (835).  No information about predation by other fish species is available.

Factors Influencing Populations: This species is known to hybridize with both B. tyrannus on the Atlantic coast and B. patronus on the Florida Gulf coast (307 737 823).  Hybrids associate with both parental species near shore, but apparently do not migrate with the schools of the large-scale menhaden (823).  Hybrids apparently do not occur in the northern Gulf of Mexico, but are relatively common south of Tampa Bay (823).  Similarly, hybrid B. smithi x B. tyrannus are rare or absent north of northeastern Florida (823).

Eggs and larvae:  Egg diameters range between 1.21 - 1.48 mm (827).  The time for hatching varies with temperature;  at 19.5 C to 21.5 C hatching occurs in 38 to 39 hours (824), above 22.0 C hatching occurs in less than 24 hours (827).  Eggs from the east Florida coast hatched in 46 hours at 18.0 C, 34 hours at 21.0 C, and 26 hours at 26.0 C (824 830).
Larvae: at hatching is about 3.0 mm SL (827).  Larvae begin transforming at around 14.0 mm SL with transformation complete between 20 and 23 mm SL (827).  Growth appears to be very rapid (831).  At 26 C in the laboratory, larvae grew 0.45 mm/day until day 20 (827)
Juveniles and adults:  Juveniles reach 160 mm FL by the end of their first summer and approximately 220 mm by the end of their second summer.  Sexual maturity is apparently attained during the second winter for most individuals (831). Mature adults differ from young adults in that their scales are more strongly serrated and their bodies are not as deep.  The largest recorded specimen is 330 mm TL (307).

sections.heading: FOOD HABITS
sections.content: The yellowfin menhaden is a filter feeder.  The diet for this species consists of phytoplankton, detritus and small zooplankton strained from the water column (1055).  Hildebrand (307) reported the presence of diatoms and sponge spicules in B. smithi stomachs.

sections.heading: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
sections.content:
Predation: B. smithi is host to the parasitic copepod, Lernaeenicus radians (307).  Called bug fish because, when in rivers, almost all individuals have parasitic crustaceans in the roof of the mouth (835).  No information about predation by other fish species is available.

Factors Influencing Populations: This species is known to hybridize with both B. tyrannus on the Atlantic coast and B. patronus on the Florida Gulf coast (307 737 823).  Hybrids associate with both parental species near shore, but apparently do not migrate with the schools of the large-scale menhaden (823).  Hybrids apparently do not occur in the northern Gulf of Mexico, but are relatively common south of Tampa Bay (823).  Similarly, hybrid B. smithi x B. tyrannus are rare or absent north of northeastern Florida (823).
